Conclusions Overall, the current study demonstrated a novel regimen composed of low-dose escitalopram oxalate and nivolumab, exhibiting a synergistic inhibitory effect on proliferation of HepG2 liver cancer cells, in particular the combination of Esc (50 μM) + Niv (20 μM) in vitro and Esc (2.5 mg/kg) + Niv (6.66 mg/kg) in vivo. Esc (50 μM) + Niv (20 μM) significantly induced apoptosis of HepG2 cells, and the combination of Esc (2.5 mg/kg) + Niv (6.66 mg/kg) significantly suppressed the growth of xenograft HepG2 tumors in nude mice. For the first time, this study indicates the potential of combinational use of low-dose escitalopram oxalate and nivolumab for inhibiting liver cancer cell proliferation, which may provide an alternative treatment for liver cancers.

1 Theoretical and Research Basis for Treatment In the United States, there are over 12 million family caregivers of persons with dementia (PWD), inclusive of Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and other neurocognitive disorders ( ). Approximately two-thirds of all family caregivers are women ( ), representing a disproportionate, gendered burden of caregiver duties. Caregiving for a PWD does not necessarily cause negative mental health outcomes and can be associated with positive factors, such as psychological growth ( ). However, family caregivers of PWD with predisposing factors, such as older age, identifying as a woman, having poorer physical health, and reporting higher subjective perceptions of strain, are at higher risk for developing mental health symptoms (e.g., caregiver burden, depression, anxiety; ). In general, caregivers of PWD report higher rates of mental health problems compared with caregivers of other illnesses (e.g., stroke) non-caregivers ( ), with 34.0% reporting depression and 43.6% reporting anxiety in prior studies ( ). These rates remained high during the COVID-19 pandemic, with 32.9% family caregivers reporting mental health problems such as depression, anxiety, or substance use over the prior month, compared with just 6.3% of respondents not in a caregiving role ( ). Caregiver burden has been conceptualized as, “the level of multifaceted strain perceived by the caregiver from caring for a family member and/or loved one over time” (p. 442; ). Burden is the result of many different types of stressors associated with the caregiving role, such as behavioral and psychiatric, physical, and cognitive symptoms of dementia; family conflict; and the type and amount of care provided by the caregiver ( ; ). Symptoms of caregiver burden vary across individuals, change over the course of the PWD’s illness, and are influenced by many factors (e.g., stage of dementia, in/dependence of the PWD, financial resources, and health of the caregiver; ; ). Family caregivers often report emotional symptoms of burden related to losses, role-related stress, uncertainty, and guilt ( ; ). Factors protecting against the development of caregiver burden, include increased social support and social engagement, greater financial resources, higher caregiver self-efficacy, and higher psychological resilience ( ; ). Family members can both mitigate and exacerbate emotional burden for the caregiver, depending on the extent of pre-existing family conflict, quality of communication, and con/discordant perceptions of care recipient’s disease/status ( ). It is important to note that caregiver burden, including its antecedents, symptoms, and assessment, remains mostly consistent across various types of dementia, including Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases ( ; ; ). Although Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a movement disorder, 80% of persons diagnosed will develop cognitive symptoms as the illness progresses, primarily in executive dysfunction, language difficulties, attentional deficits, and visuospatial deficits ( ). Compared with Alzheimer’s disease, PD is associated with higher rates of verbal agitation and physical aggression, which relate with elevated caregiver burden ( ). Yet, in general, caregiver profiles and expressions of burden are consistent across disorders and, other than illness-specific education, psychological treatments for caregiver burden do not vary ( ; ). Regardless of type of dementia, depressive and anxious symptoms reported by family caregivers of PWD have conceptual and treatment overlap with caregiver burden. Indeed, caregiver burden, depression, and anxiety tend to respond to similar psychotherapeutic treatments ( ; ). Below, we highlight two of these psychotherapeutic approaches. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Family Caregivers Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) has shown consistent positive effects on caregiver burden ( ; ; ). Further, CBT shows significant and large effects across randomized controlled trials for treatment of depression among family caregivers of PWD ( ). CBT techniques, such as cognitive restructuring, coping skills, scheduling pleasant/meaningful activities, and thought experiments, are frequently utilized in treatment studies with family caregivers to target common issues related to the caregiving role, such as limited environmental reinforcement and maladaptive thoughts ( ; ). Cognitive appraisals and subsequent thought structures have been found to be particularly impactful targets in CBT with family caregivers, as self-efficacy for managing dysfunctional thoughts has been found to be more clinically relevant for burden than improving self-efficacy in managing actual behavioral and psychiatric symptoms of PWDs ( ). Further, a study of CBT with family caregivers of PWD showed that changing maladaptive thoughts around caregiving mediated the relationship between the intervention and levels of depression ( ). This suggests that identifying and treating caregiving-specific dysfunctional thoughts and utilizing cognitive restructuring techniques is likely an effective clinical strategy for caregiver burden, depression, and anxiety symptoms among family caregivers of PWD. Caregiver Family Therapy In addition to individual-focused psychotherapies, best practices for psychological treatment with family caregivers includes a systems approach ( ), as effective caregiving for a family member with dementia requires the involvement of multiple members of a care system, usually comprised of multiple family members ( ). Caregiver Family Therapy In addition to individual-focused psychotherapies, best practices for psychological treatment with family caregivers includes a systems approach ( ), as effective caregiving for a family member with dementia requires the involvement of multiple members of a care system, usually comprised of multiple family members ( ). Caregiver Family Therapy (CFT) is a systems approach to psychotherapy wherein family caregivers take an active role in developing problem-solving approaches to providing dementia care and maintaining family functioning. A primary focus of this treatment is helping the family adapt their roles to create a stable and effective care network. Targets of CFT include three core processes for the caregiving system: (1) naming the problem and structuring care, (2) role structuring and role reverberations, and (3) caregiver self-care and widening the lens. Notably, this is a highly flexible intervention that allows the clinician to tailor to meet each caregiver’s and family’s needs ( ). Feminist Therapy In the context of family caregiving, identifying as a woman is associated with greater adoption of the caregiver role, role-related stress, and physical, emotional, and financial consequences of caregiving ( ). Therefore, a feminist-informed approach may be relevant to psychotherapy with caregivers who identify as women. Feminist therapies are often integrated into other modalities and place gender-role as a central organizing aspect of an individual’s everyday life, culture, and worldview. Therapists adopting a feminist-informed approach bring awareness to and examine the impact of gender-role socialization as well as other intersecting identities (e.g., race, queerness) on power, privilege, and oppression ( ). Through heightened awareness of internalized gender-role socialization processes and their impact, individuals are empowered to adopt more functional core beliefs and implement behavior changes that enhance self-esteem and overall mental health ( ). Although prior work has applied a feminist model to family therapy ( ), we are unaware of its application to caregivers of PWD. Together, caregivers of PWD face many challenges in providing care, managing family dynamics, and navigating a complex, fragmented healthcare system, and experiences may be shaped by gender-role. For some, the demands of being a caregiver will supersede their resources, and they may develop symptoms of caregiver burden, depression, and anxiety. Evidence-based treatments exist to help support family caregivers in gaining knowledge and skills to better balance the multidimensional demands of the caregiver role. The following case is an example of a straight White cisgender woman experiencing high levels of caregiver burden with clinically elevated symptoms of depression and anxiety in the context of caring for her spouse with PD (i.e., a cisgender man). The case integrates CBT and CFT psychotherapies, while adopting a feminist-informed approach to supplement these modalities. In doing so, we highlight the importance of blending systems-focused (i.e., CFT) and individual-focused (i.e., CBT) therapeutic approaches to caregiver burden, while maintaining a focus on the impact of gender-role socialization. 2 Case Introduction “Maude” (pseudonym) was a 68-year-old, straight, White, married, cisgender woman, referred to an outpatient mental health clinic for older adults within an academic medical center for treatment of caregiver burden. Maude was referred by a neurologist in a neuropalliative care clinic within the same academic medical center, where Maude’s husband, a cisgender man, was receiving care for advanced PD with cognitive symptoms. Maude provided informed consent upon initiation of psychotherapy. Clinically relevant benchmark scores for these measures are reported in . At intake, Maude reported clinically elevated scores on the GAI, GDS-30, and ZBI-12 (see ), but did not report PTSD symptoms (PTSD-PC = 0/5). Therefore, only the GAI, GDS-30, and ZBI-12 were administered again midway, at the end of therapy, and post-booster sessions to monitor Maude’s symptoms and treatment success. The current case primarily addressed marked distress associated with Maude’s role as a spousal caregiver. Recent changes in her spouse’s symptomology increased distress, prompting the current referral. It is not entirely clear whether pre-existing levels of depression and anxiety were clinically elevated prior to recent changes in the care recipient’s symptomology or if symptoms will persist after removal of the stressor of the caregiving role. Despite this incomplete clinical picture, a diagnosis of Adjustment Disorder with Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood (DSM-5 code: 309.28) was determined to be the best fit for this patient. Other diagnoses considered were Major Depressive Disorder and Generalized Anxiety Disorder. To address these concerns, therapy primarily consisted of CFT and CBT, while also incorporating a feminist-informed approach. Naming the Problem. Maude had a strong concept of the “problem” with her spouse. He had a PD diagnosis for about 20 years. Further, they were seen by a specialty neuropalliative care provider, who helped Maude and her spouse plan for future care. Maude worked in healthcare as a speech and language pathologist, so she had high health literacy and familiarity with PD symptoms, course, and prognosis. Although these factors do not always lead to sufficient illness knowledge and appropriate symptom appraisal, Maude made appropriate attributions of challenging behaviors (i.e., recognized hypersexuality was related to PD) and did not appear to report any denial or missing information regarding symptomology, diagnosis, or prognosis. Therefore, illness knowledge was not a major focus of therapy. Role Structuring. A poorly defined structure of care roles significantly contributed to emotional distress. Maude was the sole caregiver for her spouse and aided with most instrumental activities of daily living (e.g., finances, driving, medication, meal preparation, shopping) and a few activities of daily living, on occasion (e.g., transferring). She noted that she spends most of her time at home providing care and, when she leaves for errands, she worries about the safety of her spouse (e.g., fall risk). Maude reportedly did not receive support for any caregiving task, due in part to the pandemic as well as maladaptive cognitions about caregiving (e.g., “as a spouse, I am supposed to do everything myself”). Relatedly, Maude reported that she was not satisfied with her caregiving role as it was greater than what she wanted. This role dissatisfaction led to feelings of burnout and role entrapment, in which Maude reported losing a “sense of self”. Other than fulfilling an obligation to her spouse, Maude reported few positive aspects of her caregiving role. Maude noted that it was important for her to care for her spouse to honor their relationship. However, at this time of her life, after retirement and launching children, she hoped to spend more time exploring her own interests. Maude reported that she served the role of a caretaker for most of her adult life. She reported feelings of resentment that her adult life was so highly defined by this caregiving role. She noted that she believed her career, relationships, and sense of identity were all negatively impacted by her caregiving responsibilities throughout adulthood. Maude added that she identifies as a strong, independent women and, yet feels shame that her family and marital structure were patriarchal—exacerbating emotional distress and negative self-talk (e.g., “I am weak”). Caregiver Self-Care. Lastly, Maude reported engaging in few enjoyable activities. She noted frequently feeling socially isolated and “bored.” Further, she had difficulty defining pleasant activities in which she wanted to participate. This increased her feelings of role entrapment and negative self-talk (e.g., “I don’t even know what I like to do”), further fueling a cycle of hopelessness around her ability to incorporate self-care into her routine. Overall, from a CFT perspective, Maude has a strong illness understanding, but has structured care in a manner that is not consistent with her values or capacity. She receives little support with care, which has led to burnout as well as role entrapment. Negative emotions related to caregiving are also associated with negative self-talk (e.g., “I am weak for taking on a caregiving role”), increasing her emotional distress. Her high distress level along with an unsustainable caregiving role have contributed to limited activity engagement, fueling negative emotions and feelings of hopelessness. Taken together, Maude’s caregiver burden is a product of the structure of her caregiving role, negative thoughts and emotions, and low behavioral activation. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Conceptualization For this case, CFT was supplemented with elements of CBT to address maladaptive cognitions that were associated with negative emotions (e.g., shame, guilt, and resentment), which created barriers to changing her caregiving role and incorporating self-care. From a CBT perspective, high caregiving demands with few supports was a precipitating factor in the development of elevated depressive and anxiety symptoms. Maude held rigid intermediate beliefs about the role of a spousal caregiver, such as “the wife must provide all care for their partner.” These rigid beliefs led to maladaptive automatic thinking patterns, such as “if I don’t do everything, I am a bad spouse” (all-or-nothing thinking), “I should prioritize my family over my own needs” (should statements), and “I am weak because a strong woman would not care for someone if they didn’t want to” (all-or-nothing thinking, personalization). These maladaptive cognitions led to negative emotions, such as guilt, shame, and resentment; somatic experiences (e.g., fatigue); and behavioral avoidance for pleasant self-care activities. Feminist Therapy Conceptualization A feminist-informed approach was threaded throughout components of CFT and CBT to address the impact of gender-role socialization on the Maude’s presenting problem. Consistent with a social feminist framework of psychotherapy, we addressed the impact of internalized gender-role socialization on self-nurturance, anger, and autonomy ( ). Maude was socialized to the caregiving role at a young age, prioritizing nurturing others over herself. This aspect of gender-role socialization influenced maladaptive core beliefs that devalued her own needs (e.g., selflessness of the spousal caregiver, prioritizing and centering care recipient needs) and led to fewer self-nurturing behaviors, which also impeded upon her recognition of self (i.e., limited “sense of self”). Relatedly, the resentment she developed toward her spouse related to inequitable care roles was turned inward into self-judgements (e.g., “I am weak”). Yet, for Maude, modifying the caregiving role and increasing self-care was met with anxiety and guilt, which reflect a socialized gendered response to, as a cisgender woman, prioritize cooperation and external validation over autonomy. Thus, therapy will support Maude in increasing self-awareness regarding the impact of gender-role socialization on core beliefs about the caregiving role and herself as well as empowering Maude to accept or combat societal restraints and implement behavior change (e.g., self-care, independent activities, outward expression of anger). 7 Course of Treatment and Assessment of Progress Maude was seen for a total of 22 sessions from October 2020- July 2021. Sessions 1–8 Consistent with CFT, early in treatment, sessions focused on identifying care needs, evaluating current care roles, and identifying an extended care network. Early on, Maude was able to identify that her care role was not sustainable and included many tasks she did not value or view as important (e.g., housework). In the first few sessions, Maude started to identify which care tasks could be delegated. She contacted a home care agency to increase supports and respite as well as hired a cleaning service. During these early sessions, consistent with CBT, Maude identified maladaptive intermediate beliefs and automatic thoughts related to involving friends and adult children in care. Maude was resistant to ask others for help with caregiving tasks, noting that she did not want to “bother” her children by asking them to provide support and even concealed information from them about the care recipient’s illness symptomology and severity. In session and by using thought logs between sessions, Maude identified an intermediate belief that fueled discomfort in asking for help from her children (i.e., “parents don’t ask for help from their children”). Maude also began to identify the impact of gender-role socialization on her adoption and construction of the caregiving role (i.e., “women are caregivers”, “women caregivers don’t ask for help”). Awareness of these belief helped Maude identify and challenge cognitions that related to apprehension about including children and friends in the care network. Eventually, Maude asked her children to call their father weekly to provide him with emotional support and accepted offers from friends to cook her and her spouse dinner. By the eighth session, supports for care tasks were being implemented and Maude reported some declines in depression, anxiety, and caregiver burden ( ). Sessions 9–14 In the middle stages, therapy focused on Maude’s sense of identity, to address feelings of role entrapment as well as to inform behaviors to target for behavioral activation. Maude reported feeling as though she did not have a strong “sense of self” and struggled to identify pleasant activities she would like to incorporate with increased respite. Sessions utilized values assessments to attempt to understand core components of Maude’s identity. Linking personal values to a sense of identity and behaviors was challenging for Maude. During these sessions, Maude reported that she felt like a “weak woman” for not having a strong “sense of self” and noted that she felt this “weakness” for much of her adult life. To address this, therapy incorporated components of CBT (e.g., how this belief influenced thoughts, emotions, and behaviors) as well as Feminist Therapy (e.g., impact of gender-role socialization and power on beliefs and mental health). Maude identified and named how internalized gender-role socialization shaped her core beliefs. She then began to frame self-care as a “radical act” and a “social justice issue” to combat oppressive patriarchal social structures that impede upon self-nurturance and self-recognition for women. For example, a session involved identifying feminist role models to evaluate how they combated oppressive structures and biased messages to pursue their own self-directed activities. This framing appeared to motivate Maude for greater action and sessions became an outlet for Maude to express anger outwardly. During these sessions, Maude also identified that she wanted to engage in more solo behaviors that would produce a “sense of adventure,” as this was a neglected component of her identity. Eventually, she reported that she wanted to take a vacation abroad without her spouse and this became her long-term behavioral goal. After 14 sessions, Maude continued to evidence decreases in anxiety, depression, and caregiver burden ( ), and showed an increased motivation for behavior change. Sessions 15–20 In the later stages, therapy focused on behavioral activation. Maude identified smaller “adventurous” activities and solo activities to incorporate in her schedule each week (e.g., calling an old friend she lost contact with and asking them out for coffee, solo walks or drives). In addition, she set smaller goals related to her long-term goal of a trip abroad without her spouse (e.g., create an itinerary, get quotes from travel agencies). As Maude incorporated these activities into her schedule, she reported an increase in feelings of guilt for wanting to spend more time away from her spouse. To address these emotions, in therapy, she continued to identify maladaptive beliefs and cognitions that led to these negative emotions (e.g., “I am a bad partner, if I have experiences without my spouse”, “women must be cooperative and not offend their spouse”). Maude continued to utilize weekly thought logs as homework to identify and challenge maladaptive beliefs and cognitions. Progress on Therapy Goals At the conclusion of 20 sessions, Maude had successfully incorporated home care and accepted support from friends. She also increased the role of her children in providing emotional support for her spouse with PD. These activities increased opportunities for respite and helped her feel less “trapped” in her caregiver role. The bulk of therapy focused on addressing maladaptive beliefs and cognitions that fueled negative emotions (e.g., shame, guilt, resentment) and behavioral deactivation. By questioning rigid beliefs about marriage, family, caregiving, and gender-role, Maude was able to identify and challenge maladaptive cognitions, which also increased her motivation for behavior change. Although therapy ended before Maude reached her long-term goal of traveling by herself, she was more confident that she would be able to regulate negative emotions associated with pursuing this behavioral goal. Further, Maude self-reported that at the conclusion of therapy she had a clear “sense of self,” noting that this was the first time in her adult life she was confident about being able to articulate aspects of her identity. Assessment of Progress Maude’s progress in therapy was quantitatively assessed via the reduction in her psychological symptoms: anxiety, depression, and caregiver burden. Quantitative assessment was conducted at the first session, midway (12 sessions), end of therapy (20 sessions), and immediately following two booster sessions (22 sessions). As shown in , Maude experienced a decrease in all tracked symptoms across the course of therapy. Specifically, from the start of therapy to discharge (22 sessions), Maude reported reductions in anxiety (GAI = −4), depression (GDS-30 = −12), and caregiver burden (ZBI-12: −21). To the authors’ knowledge, none of these measures have minimal clinically important difference scores available. 8 Complicating Factors There are various cultural considerations that accompany work with caregivers, as the caregiving experience is rooted in cultural and familial contexts. In addition, her sons went to college and moved away from home for their careers. These factors impacted care roles, care networks, and communication patterns, as Maude did not want to “burden” her adult children who were living independently. Another complicating familial factor was that communication about emotionally-laden topics was often avoided in favor of maintaining the status quo, which was evident in the caregiver role with her spouse and her discomfort expressing her challenges to her adult sons. Relatedly, the family was structured in a patriarchal manner, in which the care recipient (husband) often was the primary decision-maker. This dynamic complicated the caregiving role because, at times, Maude reported feeling uncomfortable making decisions without consensus. It is clear that her gender-role socialization was an important factor in Maude’s presenting problem and treatment. As mentioned, a feminist therapy approach was adopted throughout treatment to address the impact of gender-role socialization on the caregiving role and Maude’s mental health. The therapist in the current case identified as a White cisgender man. Therefore, it was important to consider power dynamics within the therapeutic relationship to promote an egalitarian relationship. Part of this involved openly discussing trust, rapport, and comfort when discussing gender in session. Maude repeatedly noted she was comfortable discussing these topics and noted it was empowering to express anger about the patriarchy to a man. It is important to note Maude’s intersecting identities (i.e., straight, White, cisgender, and middle-class) that influence her experiences with power, privilege, and oppression, which is further discussed in Recommendations to Clinicians and Students. Another complicating factor is that this treatment took place during the COVID-19 pandemic. Although many social activities had resumed with social distancing, comfort levels for in-person social interaction varied. For this reason, Maude was hesitant to seek in-person social support within her neighborhood, as she identified her husband as “high risk” and noted many of her neighbors were older adults and, thus, also “high risk”. To address this, psychotherapy, which was delivered remotely via secure live video, focused on goal-setting for pleasant activities that were within Maud’s comfort levels and recommended public health guidelines. 9 Access and Barriers to Care Maude had social and economic resources that promoted her access to care. Notably, Maude’s financial standing influenced the course of therapy, particularly related to extending her care network to professionals for respite (e.g., paying for home care and cleaning services). Further, her goals involved traveling, which also reflected her ability to secure financial resources for expenses as well as financial and social capital for respite. These factors should be noted as they may not translate to other caregivers, particularly those with limited social and/or economic resources. Relatedly, Maude was well-connected to medical providers, both for her spouse with PD and for herself. She referred to the current clinic by a neurologist within the same large healthcare system/academic medical center. Often for family caregivers, such as with this case, it is the PWD that is seen as a patient within the medical system and the caregiver is referred after disclosing stress or emotional challenges to the PWD’s provider. The ability for the psychologist and neurologist to closely collaborate within a single academic medical center (e.g., sharing patients, serving on committees together), facilitates these types of referrals, which may not generalize to all neurology clinics. In addition to access, this type of referral process also has ethical considerations, as referrals are typically placed within an electronic health record via the PWD’s chart (i.e., the patient of the encounter in which the referral was placed), not the caregiver. For this reason, Maude and her therapist set clear expectations about the therapist’s role on her husband’s care team. For example, rather than doing a chart review in her husband’s chart, the therapist directed Maude to summarize visit notes or share copies of reports. Another example is that Maude was encouraged to contact the neurologist with any relevant information that emerged within psychotherapy sessions (e.g., realization that care recipient anxiety was elevated). The therapist did, however, offer to serve as a liaison to the neurologist, if needed, given how closely these two clinics worked together. 10 Follow-Up After 20 sessions, Maude reported that she had met her therapy goals and was self-reporting less emotional distress and higher self-efficacy. In addition, her screens remained stable from mid-therapy improvements, albeit still clinically elevated. Maude agreed that she had accumulated skills in treatment to continue to manage her distress independently. Further, she

This data, along with her self-reported symptom stability, related to her self-efficacy for emotional distress management. Therefore, she was confident that she would continue to manage caregiver burden, depression, and anxiety symptoms upon discharge. 11 Treatment Implications of the Case This case describes the application of CFT, supplemented with components of CBT as well as feminist therapy, to address caregiving-related distress (caregiver burden) among a family caregiver of a spouse with PD. Caregiving for a family member is a process rooted in the family system and/or long-standing relational dynamics with the care recipient as well as others providing care ( ). The theoretical background of CFT values the family system and relational component to caregiving and its associations with psychological challenges for the caregiver ( ). Yet, CFT has received little attention in clinical research trials. Therefore, this case adds to the literature by providing insights into this psychotherapeutic modality and its application in clinical care. CBT is considered the gold standard for psychotherapy with caregivers of PWD ( ). In particular, cognitive aspects of this model (e.g., maladaptive thinking patterns, core beliefs) align well with caregiving-related challenges to the caregiving role, caregiver-care recipient relationship, and family context. Further, given the relevance of gender-role socialization to this case, a feminist-informed approach was threaded throughout to further supplement CFT and CBT. This case highlights the ways in which these psychotherapy modalities (i.e., CFT, a systems-focused approach, and CBT, an individual-focused approach) can be used to complement one another. This case highlights the role of gender in psychotherapy with family caregivers. As discussed, the overwhelming majority of caregivers are women ( ). Further, caregiving is a gendered role, with gender differences noted in care responsibilities, help-seeking behaviors, expression of burden, and beliefs about caregiving ( ). Indeed, women experience higher rates of caregiver burden and more negative impacts of the caregiving role on their life ( ). Importantly, intersecting identities influence these roles and outcomes. In this case example, Maude, a straight White cisgender woman, clearly articulated the ways in which her various caregiver roles impacted her life (e.g., missed opportunities for professional advancement) and presenting problem. In particular, gender-role socialization had a role in shaping maladaptive core beliefs and thoughts (e.g., “the wife must provide all care for their partner”, “weak women assume the caregiving role”) as well as increasing feelings of hopelessness, guilt, shame, and resentment. A feminist-informed approach aligned well with the main therapeutic modalities. For example, in CFT, psychotherapy can explore the ways in which gender-role socialization influences role structuring. In CBT, psychotherapy can address maladaptive core beliefs related to gender-role socialization. While gender disparities are well-researched in public health, this topic receives less attention in psychological intervention research, as an explicit topic to address in psychotherapy. This case highlights one way in which gender can be addressed in psychotherapy with family caregivers. It should be noted, however, that Maude’s intersecting identities, which primarily reflected social power and privilege, likely led to a greater emphasis on her identity as a woman. 12 Recommendations to Clinicians and Students First, we recommend that clinicians and students consider combining psychotherapeutic approaches that appreciate both individual as well as systems frameworks for work with family caregivers. In this case, both CBT and CFT were used, which provided a thorough conceptualization and treatment approach for addressing individual challenges (e.g., maladaptive thoughts, behavioral deactivation) as well as family systems and structuring the caregiving role with the broader care network. These latter components are essential to consider for clinicians specializing in psychotherapy with caregivers. Second, we recommend that clinicians and students balance transdiagnostic features of psychotherapeutic approaches and illness knowledge of specific neurocognitive disorders. Although Maude was caring for a spouse with PD, many of the psychotherapeutic techniques used for this case were developed with caregivers of people with Alzheimer’s disease. These treatments commonly apply across neurocognitive disorders. However, it was important for the therapeutic alliance that Maude felt the clinician understood the course, prognosis, and symptomology of PD. This was particularly important in the context of challenging behavioral symptoms (e.g., hypersexual and compulsive behaviors). Yet, case conceptualization and treatment targets in this case were transdiagnostic and could have been applied to a number of neurocognitive disorders. Third, as mentioned, gender was a major component of this case. We strongly recommend that clinicians and students working with caregivers incorporate opportunities to explore gender in psychotherapy (e.g., societal norms, hierarchies, internalized views). Although relevant, the role of gender may not always be explicitly addressed in psychotherapy with caregivers. We advocate for manualized treatments, study protocols, and specialized training programs to highlight opportunities for clinicians to address the role of gender in psychological distress among family caregivers within an evidence-based psychotherapy model. Lastly, and relatedly, we advocate for an intersectional approach to conceptualizing and incorporating aspects of feminist therapy into treatment with caregivers. Intersecting identities, including but not limited to, sexual and gender identity, race and ethnicity, class, and disability, influence experiences of power, privilege, and oppression in everyday life. Thus, these intersecting identities also heavily influence the caregiver role, role-related stressors, core beliefs, and mental health. Adopting an intersectional approach in psychotherapy is needed. Of note, particularly among older generations, women of color may have negative experiences with the feminist movement, which should be considered ( ).

INTRODUCTION Tobacco use is the leading cause of preventable death in the U.S., and American Indian/Alaska Native (AI/AN) people have a higher prevalence of tobacco use and tobacco-related diseases than the general population. , Thus, effective smoking cessation programs and methods to reduce cigarette use among AI/AN individuals are important public health initiatives. Although several U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)–approved products and evidence-based interventions exist for smoking cessation, , individuals who smoke have increasingly used E-cigarettes, which are nonapproved FDA products, as smoking cessation aids. , Data from the 2018 National Health Interview Survey found that >49% of individuals who reported currently using cigarettes also reported lifetime E-cigarette use, and 9.7% reported currently using E-cigarettes. Research has indicated that AI/AN individuals may use E-cigarettes more often than other groups. For example, data from the 2021 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System indicated that current use among AI/AN individuals (8.7%) was higher than that among Asian individuals (4.7%), Black individuals (5.5%), and Hispanic individuals (4.6%). However, use among AI/AN people was lower than among Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander persons (10.7%) but has prevalence similar to that among non-Hispanic White individuals (8.2%). Moreover, according to Oklahoma 2020 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System data, current E-cigarette use was higher among the AI/AN population than among non-Hispanic White population (11.0% vs 8.9%). The uptick of E-cigarette use among persons who smoke is not surprising because E-cigarettes are often used as harm-reduction devices and smoking cessation aids because they have lower levels of carcinogens than cigarettes. , Recent research regarding the efficacy of E-cigarette use has shown that E-cigarette use may be beneficial in increasing smoking cessation rates, particularly when compared with nicotine replacement therapy (NRT). However, the prevalence of continued cigarette use among those who use E-cigarettes is high. Furthermore, some research indicates that dual use of E-cigarettes and cigarettes may increase harms related to tobacco use. Finally, although studies have not shown E-cigarettes to have serious adverse health events compared with other smoking-cessation methods, concerns remain regarding the long-term use of E-cigarettes, and studies evaluating long-term health effects are still needed. Although E-cigarettes have not been FDA approved for smoking cessation, interventions such as NRT, group therapy, prescription medication (i.e., bupropion and varenicline), advice from physicians, individual counseling, and other self-help interventions are strategies that have been identified as effective compared with no or minimal interventions or have been approved by the FDA. , , Studies have found that AI/AN people who smoke have a lower rate of quitting smoking than other groups, , but one cohort study from 1990–1994 found high cessation rates among older American Indian individuals. Among AI/AN persons who smoke, access issues related to cessation interventions, distrust toward healthcare providers, lack of pharmacotherapy safety awareness, and lack of knowledge of pharmacotherapy benefits have led to decreased utilization of evidence-based treatments. , , , Thus, smoking cessation patterns among AI/AN persons who smoke may not be comparable with those among other populations, and examination of cessation among this population is necessary. Individuals who use E-cigarettes are more likely to have previous cigarette-cessation attempts, , and E-cigarettes are most often used for smoking cessation. , However, one unanswered question is since the advent of E-cigarettes, whether people who smoke and use E-cigarettes are using them instead of recommended evidence-based methods or whether they are using them in addition to recommended evidence-based methods. This question is important among AI/AN populations because many have higher rates of cigarette and E-cigarette use, , , have increased tobacco-related diseases, and have lower utilization of evidence-based methods. , Thus, the authors use exploratory methods to obtain preliminary data to better generate a hypothesis regarding the impact of E-cigarettes on the use of evidence-based methods. The primary objective of this study was to assess the associations between E-cigarette use (current, past, or never) and the use of evidence-based smoking cessation methods in a sample of American Indian adults who smoke cigarettes. Research staff obtained informed consent from all participants, and participants received a $20 department store gift card. Participants completed a survey that included questions on cigarette and E-cigarette use, cessation behaviors, other tobacco use, reasons for E-cigarette use, risk perceptions of tobacco products, and demographic information. Because this study aimed to evaluate cessation behaviors, research staff collected saliva and carbon monoxide breath samples. Investigators have published details of the setting, sample, baseline recruitment and data collection methods, eligibility, and baseline results elsewhere. All participants were asked whether they ever tried to quit smoking. They were also asked about previous cessation methods used. Only participants who answered yes to the quit attempt question or indicated the use of at least 1 cessation method were included in this analysis. For the original study, research staff screened and enrolled 375 individuals into the study. The majority of potential participants self-screened by reading information about the study on flyers and did not complete a screening assessment form. Therefore, the total number of potential participants screened is not available. Among the original study participants, 289 (77%) individuals indicated a previous cessation attempt or use of a cessation method and were included in this study. The study analysis occurred in 2023. The Cherokee Nation and University of Oklahoma Health Sciences Center IRBs (#274 and #5970, respectively) approved this study. Cherokee Nation IRB approved the publication of this manuscript. Measures The main dependent variables were the cessation methods used the last time participants tried to quit smoking, regardless of when that quit attempt occurred. Participants were provided a matrix question about previous cessation methods used with an option of yes/no for each method. The smoking cessation methods were not mutually exclusive. Participants had the opportunity to mark yes or no to all methods used in their previous quit attempt. The authors detail below how smoking cessation methods were categorized and grouped. For this analysis, the authors evaluated NRT, prescription medication, and cold turkey methods. The authors also inquired about traditional or Native cessation methods and other assistance such as smoking cessation counseling or classes. Owing to the low number of responses to these methods, they were excluded from analyses. E-cigarette use for smoking cessation was also included but was excluded as an outcome variable because it is the main independent variable of interest. Participants were asked about the use of nicotine patches, gum, lozenge, or spray. If participants indicated the use of any of the products mentioned earlier, they were categorized as having used NRT (yes). If participants answered no to all nicotine products, they were categorized as having not used NRT (no). If participants checked no to one option but left the other options blank, they were excluded from the analysis. Participants were asked about using Zyban (bupropion) or Chantix (varenicline). If participants indicated the use of either medication, they were categorized as having used prescription medication (yes). If participants answered no to using both medications, they were categorized as having not used medication (no). If participants checked no to one option but left the second option blank, they were excluded from the analysis. Participants were asked about using the cold turkey method (stopped all at once). If participants answered yes to this question, they were categorized as having used the cold turkey method (yes). If participants answered no, they were categorized as having not used the cold turkey method (no). If participants did not check yes or no for this question, they were excluded from the analysis. The main independent variable was E-cigarette use. The status of E-cigarette use at baseline was assessed with the following question: Have you ever vaped or used an e-cig, even one or two times? Respondents were given the option of yes/no. Participants were then asked whether they used E-cigarettes during the past 30 days. Individuals were considered to be currently using E-cigarettes if they had ever used E-cigarettes and used them within the past 30 days. Study participants were considered to have used E-cigarettes in the past if they indicated ever use of E-cigarettes but not within the past 30 days. The use of E-cigarettes, cigarettes, NRT, and/or prescription medication has been found to vary by demographics. , , , Furthermore, smoking behaviors, including other tobacco use, cigarettes per day, nicotine dependence, quit attempts, and intentions to quit, have been associated with E-cigarette use, NRT, and/or prescription medication. , , , , , Therefore, to control for potential confounding variables, the authors included the variables below. Age groupings were categorized as 18–44 years and ≥45 years. Gender was categorized as male or female. Education was defined as the highest level of school completed and categorized as less than high school, high school graduate/GED, or greater than high school. Household income was defined as annual household income from all sources and was categorized as $0–$15,000, $15,001–30,000, or ≥$30,001. Marital status was categorized as married, unmarried living with a partner, single, or divorced/separated/widowed. Other tobacco use was based on cigar, cigarillo, filtered cigar, hookah, or dissolvable tobacco use. Participants who reported daily, weekly, or monthly use of the products listed earlier were categorized as currently using other tobacco products. Individuals who reported ever using these products but not currently were categorized as using these products in the past, and participants who reported never using these products were categorized as never using. Cigarette packs per day was based on self-reported average number of cigarettes smoked per day. Cigarette packs per day was used rather than cigarettes smoked per day owing to the clustering of responses at 20 cigarettes and 10 cigarettes. If individuals reported smoking 20 or more cigarettes a day, they were classified as having smoked ≥1 packs per day. Otherwise, they were categorized as having smoked <1 pack per day. Salivary cotinine level (ng/mL) was assayed using a Salimetrics Salivary Cotinine ELISA kit as described elsewhere. All salivary samples ran in duplicate, with results reported as mean values of each duplicate set. Confidence to quit smoking was based on the question, How confident are you that you will quit smoking within the next month? Responses consisted of a range on a ladder scale with 0=not at all confident and 10=very confident. Individuals who reported having stopped smoking for 1 day or longer within the past 12 months because they were trying to quit were categorized as having a quit attempt within the past 12 months (yes). Otherwise, they were categorized as no. Number of lifetime quit attempts was based on self-reported number of times an individual attempted to quit smoking. Individuals who reported a likelihood of quitting within the next 30 days or the next 6 months were classified as intending to quit smoking (yes). Individuals who reported a likelihood of quitting within a year or more than a year or not likely to quit smoking were classified as not intending to quit smoking (no). Statistical Analysis Continuous variables were summarized with mean, SD, median, IQR, and range and compared within cessation method usage (yes versus no) using 2-sample t -tests or Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, with the latter being employed when the assumption of normality was violated. Categorical variables were summarized with count and percentage and compared using chi-square tests for independence or Fisher's exact test in the case of low expected cell counts (<5) or zero cells. Each cessation method was considered as an outcome (yes versus no) in a logistic regression setting. ORs were reported for each predictor in isolation as well as AORs for other predictors in the saturated model, without interaction terms, given limited cell counts for some combinations of cessation method and E-cigarette usage group. The models were run using complete-case analysis given the low rate of missingness. Statistical significance was defined with α=0.05 (2 sided). All analyses were conducted using R, Version 4.3.1. RESULTS presents the characteristics of the 289 participants with complete data and reported a previous cessation attempt. Among these, 55% were aged from 18 to 44 years, 64% were female, 45% had more than a high school education, 78% had an income <$30,000 per year, and 61% were married or living with a partner. Among the participants, 18% reported current E-cigarette use, and 50% indicated past E-cigarette use. Overall, the mean cotinine level for all participants was 384.8 ng/mL (SD= ±356.8). In terms of cessation, participants, overall, had a mean confidence to quit smoking score of 2.9 (SD= ±2.8), 40% of participants had attempted to quit tobacco use in the prior 12 months, the average number of lifetime quit attempts was 5.8 (SD= ±15.3), and 31% indicated an intent to quit cigarettes within 6 months or sooner. For the cessation method used during the most recent quit attempt, 40% indicated NRT use, 19% reported prescription medication use, and 55% reported using the cold turkey method. also presents the characteristics of the population by cessation methods used during the most recent quit attempt. For NRT, factors significantly ( p <0.05) associated with use included age, cotinine levels, cigarette packs per day, and E-cigarette use. Although <33% of those aged 18–44 years used NRT, nearly 48% of those aged ≥45 years used NRT. Individuals who used NRT had a cotinine level of 463.6 ng/mL (SD ±374.3) compared with 334.3 ng/mL (SD ±337.2) among those who did not use NRT. More than 50% of individuals who smoked 1 or more cigarette packs per day reported NRT use, compared with only 33% of individuals who smoked <1 pack per day. Regarding E-cigarette use, almost 50% of individuals who used E-cigarettes either currently or in the past reported NRT use, compared with only 21% of participants who never used E-cigarettes. For the use of prescription medications for cessation, the only characteristics significantly associated with use were age, cotinine levels, and E-cigarette use ( p <0.05). Individuals with higher cotinine levels were more likely to report use of prescription medication than individuals with lower levels of cotinine. Roughly one quarter of individuals who currently or formerly used E-cigarettes also reported the use of prescription medication, compared with only 10% of participants who reported never using E-cigarettes. For the cold turkey method, younger individuals, individuals who smoked <1 pack of cigarettes per day, individuals with lower cotinine levels, and participants with a quit attempt in the past 12 months reported this method compared with their counterparts ( p <0.05). Finally, 70% of individuals who never used E-cigarettes reported trying the cold turkey method compared with 49% of participants who used E-cigarette in the past and 50% of those currently using E-cigarettes. , , show the unadjusted and adjusted analyses of E-cigarette use associated with the use of NRT, prescription medication, and the cold turkey method. Individuals who currently or formerly used E-cigarettes were more likely to report using NRT than participants who never used E-cigarettes ( p <0.001) ( ). After adjusting for covariates, current and past E-cigarette use was not significantly associated with the use of prescription medication ( p <0.05) ( ). In contrast, individuals reporting current or past use of E-cigarettes were significantly much less likely to report using the cold turkey method than those who never used E-cigarettes ( p <0.01). DISCUSSION For this study, the authors aimed to understand the association between E-cigarette use and the use of evidence-based smoking cessation methods. In this sample of American Indian adults who smoke and who had a previous smoking quit attempt, participants who previously or currently used E-cigarettes were more likely to report the use of NRT and less likely to report using the cold turkey method. The results suggest that individuals who currently or previously used E-cigarettes may have used NRT as a smoking cessation method more often than those who never used E-cigarettes. In addition, individuals who never used E-cigarettes more often used the cold turkey method in previous quit attempts than those who used E-cigarettes. Among this cohort of American Indian persons who smoke, 2 general groups are apparent: persons who tended to use a form of nicotine replacement (including E-cigarettes) to help quit smoking and those who did not. Reasons for these associations, including personal preference, access to NRT/E-cigarettes, and inability to afford other methods, deserve additional study. Reasons for these associations, including personal preference, access to NRT/E-cigarettes, and inability to afford other methods, deserve additional study. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate the association between E-cigarette use and the use of evidence-based smoking cessation methods among an American Indian population. The results of this cross-sectional study appear to contrast with those of a previous longitudinal cohort study that concluded that E-cigarette use did not influence the future use of evidence-based smoking cessation products. However, the comparison between the present study and the aforementioned study is limited owing to the differences in study design. Even though E-cigarettes have not been FDA approved as a smoking cessation method, many individuals who use E-cigarettes are nonetheless using them to reduce or quit cigarette smoking. , This study showed that AI/AN individuals who have used E-cigarettes were more likely to report previous use of NRT. Use of NRT may indicate susceptibility to cessation failure. For example, previous research has shown that individuals who used NRT had stronger cravings, more nicotine withdrawals, and higher nicotine dependence than those who did not use NRT. Thus, individuals who choose to use NRT may be more likely to experience unsuccessful cessation attempts. Individuals who have used NRT as a method may be more likely to try E-cigarettes given that previous use of NRT did not culminate in sustained smoking cessation. The opposite may be true for those who indicated the use of the cold turkey method. A previous study analyzing the 2010–2011 Tobacco Use Supplement to the Current Population Survey found that among individuals who previously smoked, those who were less nicotine dependent before quitting had higher odds of reporting unassisted quitting than individuals who quit utilizing pharmacologic methods. Therefore, those who have previously tried the cold turkey method may be less nicotine dependent than those who used pharmacologic methods and may be less likely to try E-cigarette use when attempting cessation. Further studies should assess reasons why individuals who use E-cigarettes also choose to use NRT and how that relates to cessation success. This may be especially important to research given that a recent Cochrane review found that the use of E-cigarettes with nicotine was more effective for cessation than NRT. It is also important to study how E-cigarette use may affect the future use of recommended evidence-based methods. If E-cigarette use hinders the future use of evidence-based methods, more targeted approaches may be needed for individuals who use E-cigarettes, especially among AI/AN populations. Although a previous study indicated that E-cigarette use did not affect future cessation methods, it did not include AI/AN individuals and was focused on the context of chronic disease. Because the present study was a cross-sectional study, the authors were unable to determine the directionality of E-cigarette use in relation to evidence-based methods. Cessation behaviors among individuals who use E-cigarettes may differ from the behaviors among those do not use E-cigarettes. As such, more research is needed to better understand the association between E-cigarette use and evidence-based methods, particularly the impact on future cessation attempts. Limitations This study has some limitations. This was a cross-sectional analysis, and the temporal relationship of associations cannot be determined. Participants consisted of a clinic-based convenience sample and not a sample of the general population. Selection bias may have been introduced and may affect the generalizability of results. Despite this limitation, the clinic setting may be an ideal setting for future follow-up research and tobacco cessation interventions. Because this was a convenience sample of AI/AN adults recruited from a single clinic in Oklahoma, the results of this study may not be generalizable to other AI/AN populations in the U.S. Survey data were self-reported and subject to recall bias. Cessation methods were not mutually exclusive. Individuals could have reported the use of multiple cessation methods. Furthermore, the authors were unable to evaluate combined therapies such as NRT/behavioral counseling and medication/behavioral counseling. Combination therapies are more effective than stand-alone treatments. Because this was a secondary data analysis, the authors were unable to control for the use of other substances, such as lifetime use of alcohol, cannabis, or other drugs. Therefore, the authors could not control for these potential confounders. In addition, the authors only inquired about the most recent smoking cessation attempt. Thus, the authors did not know the cessation methods ever used among the study population and were unable to account for lifetime use of cessation methods. Individuals who use E-cigarettes for cessation purposes may differ in cessation behaviors from individuals who use E-cigarettes for social reasons (i.e., preferred flavorings, use where smoking is not allowed, or family/friends use of E-cigarettes). The next study to assess the association between E-cigarette use and evidence-based methods should consider these potential differences and account for such differences in the analyses. CONCLUSIONS Current and past E-cigarette use was associated with NRT, whereas never use was associated with the cold turkey method. A larger study is needed to determine whether E-cigarette users are also more likely to have tried prescription medication for smoking cessation. Whether or not the use of E-cigarettes influences the future use of evidence-based cessation attempts in this population is unknown. Future studies should evaluate this association further because it may be beneficial in developing interventions for American Indian people who smoke and the broader general population. 1. Introduction Group A Streptococcus (GAS, Streptococcus pyogenes ) is a Gram-positive exclusively human pathogen that is responsible for a wide range of diseases. These include skin and soft tissue infections, like pharyngitis, impetigo and erysipelas [ ], and more invasive diseases such as necrotising fasciitis [ ] and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome [ ]. There has been a notable global increase in the incidences of severe invasive GAS infections since the late 1980s [ , ]. Around 15 years ago, scarlet fever, a disease associated with significant morbidity and mortality that had almost completely disappeared by the end of the twentieth century, re-emerged with outbreaks reported in China, Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore, and the United Kingdom [ , , ]. Untreated pharyngitis/tonsillitis can also lead to autoimmune sequelae acute rheumatic fever (ARF) and rheumatic heart disease (RHD) [ , ]. Another autoimmune complication, acute glomerulonephritis (AGN), is associated with impetigo [ ]. It was estimated that a minimum of 18.1 million people suffer from severe GAS diseases, with an additional 1.78 million incident cases occurring each year. Annually, over 517,000 people die from severe GAS infections. In addition, over 111 million cases of streptococcal pyoderma and 616 million cases of GAS pharyngitis are reported each year [ , ]. Although invasive GAS infection rates dropped during the COVID-19 pandemic, a sharp increase in incidence and severity of invasive GAS infections was reported after the pandemic [ , , , ]. The greatest burden of GAS disease is due to RHD, with a prevalence of at least 15.6 million cases, 282,000 new cases, and 233,000 deaths each year [ ]. GAS genes that encode M protein and T antigens display the highest levels of sequence diversity, giving rise to the two primary serological typing schemes historically used to define strains, as well as the subsequent genotyping system that is more commonly used nowadays. The N-terminal amino acid sequence of the surface-exposed M protein is epidemiologically classified into more than 100 M serotypes, which show differing patterns of regional and global distribution. However, serotyping has been mostly replaced by emm -genotyping, with over 200 emm -types [ ]. T-typing is based on the trypsin-resistant heteropolymers (T antigens) that form the elongated pilus fibre [ ]. Recently, a new genotyping scheme for pilus adhesin and pilus fibre (T antigen) genes was developed and combined with emm typing to provide a more accurate account of the global GAS strain population [ ]. There is currently no licenced vaccine against GAS, but several vaccine candidates are in the development pipeline, and some have passed early clinical trials [ , ]. GAS is generally treatable with standard antibiotics, but there have been reports about increasing resistance to macrolides and tetracycline. High macrolide resistance is mainly due to ribosomal target modifications encoded by erm genes, ribosomal alterations, and active efflux pumps that regulate antibiotic entry due to mefA/E and msrD genes. Tetracycline resistance arises from tet gene expression, whereas combined tetracycline/macrolide resistance is usually linked with the insertion of ermB into the transposon carrying tetM [ ]. GAS is generally still highly sensitive to beta-lactam antibiotics such as penicillin. However, two related GAS strains have been identified that showed reduced susceptibility to ampicillin, amoxicillin, and cefotaxime [ ]. In a follow-up study, 137 geographically widespread GAS strains were found to carry mutations in the pbp2x gene, encoding penicillin-binding protein 2X (PBP2X), which has a lower affinity for beta-lactams [ ]. GAS produces a large arsenal of secreted and cell surface-associated virulence factors that contribute to the pathogenesis of infection. These include adhesins, cytolysins, superantigens, spreading factors, and immune evasion factors. This review provides an overview of GAS virulence factors with a focus on novel insights and the vaccine landscape reported over recent years. 2. Secreted GAS Virulence Factors GAS secretes a large arsenal of virulence to evade immunity, degrade tissue, and spread, including lysing host cells, disabling immune signals (chemokines and complement), breaking down neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), and causing systemic effects like toxic shock ( ). 2.1. Superantigens (SAgs) Superantigens (SAgs) are a family of structurally related T cell mitogens produced by GAS and a few other Gram-positive cocci. A hallmark of SAgs is their ability to simultaneously bind to major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II on antigens presenting cells and the T cell receptor (TcR) on T cells. In contrast to conventional peptide antigens, superantigens bind to MHC class II outside the peptide-binding groove, and sequentially bind the TcR via the variable region of the TcR b-chain, stimulating up to 25% of an individual’s T cell population. The oligoclonal stimulation of T cells and antigen-presenting cells (APCs) by SAgs results in a massive release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as tumour necrosis factor (TNF), interleukin 1-beta (IL-1b), and T cell mediators, such as IL-2,

In contrast to conventional peptide antigens, superantigens bind to MHC class II outside the peptide-binding groove, and sequentially bind the TcR via the variable region of the TcR b-chain, stimulating up to 25% of an individual’s T cell population. The oligoclonal stimulation of T cells and antigen-presenting cells (APCs) by SAgs results in a massive release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as tumour necrosis factor (TNF), interleukin 1-beta (IL-1b), and T cell mediators, such as IL-2, which can lead to fever and shock [ ]. CD28, the general co-stimulatory receptor, which is constitutively expressed on T cells and interacts with B7 molecules (CD80 and CD86), has been identified as an additional and essential receptor for cytokine production [ ]. It was also shown that SAgs that bind to the MHC class II b-chain, such as SMEZ, also bind directly to CD28 and B7, enhancing B7/CD28 costimulatory axis formation, which is crucial for T cell activation [ ]. SAg activation has also been shown to engage mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells, which respond by releasing high levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines [ ]. Streptococcal SAgs have been implicated in a range of human diseases, most notably, toxic shock syndrome and scarlet fever [ ]. Currently, there are 13 known superantigens produced by GAS, which include the streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins (Spe) A, C, G-M, R, and Q, streptococcal superantigen (SSA), and streptococcal mitogenic exotoxin Z (SMEZ) [ ]. Three of them (SpeA, SpeC, and SSA) have been associated with increased fitness and virulence of contemporary GAS strains causing scarlet fever and invasive disease [ , ]. Those strains harbour a prophage that, in addition to sag genes, also carries genes expressing the secreted DNase Spd1 and the cytolysin streptolysin O (SLO). Spd1 was found to act synergistically with SpeC to facilitate nasopharyngeal colonisation, whereas SLO induced glutathione efflux, which promotes SSA release and activity [ ]. A recent study has shown that a new variant of the GAS serotype M1 (designated ‘M1UK’), which has been linked with seasonal scarlet fever surges in the U.K., exhibited enhanced expression of SpeA. This was due to a single SNP in the 5′ transcriptional leader sequence of the transfer-messenger RNA gene ssrA that drives enhanced SpeA expression as a result of ssrA terminator read-through [ ]. SpeA was also shown to play an important role in acute nasopharyngeal infection using transgenic mice that express human MHC class II molecules as a SAg-sensitive infection model, where GAS infection was strongly enhanced in mice that express HLA-DQ8 or HLA-DR4 [ ]. Furthermore, SAg-dependent, Vβ8-specific T cell activation in the cervical lymph nodes was observed during GAS infection and these Vβ8-specific T cells were required for efficient nasopharyngeal infection, as mice vaccinated with SpeA rendered Vβ8-specific T cells poorly responsive, resulting in reduced infection [ ]. In tonsillar tissue, SpeA exposure triggers B cell apoptosis and markedly reduces Ig production, thereby weakening the humoral immune response. In SpeA-stimulated cultures, T follicular helper cells downregulated C-X-C chemokine receptor 5 while upregulating OX40, an inducible T cell co-stimulator. This altered Tfh phenotype correlated with impaired chemotaxis toward CXCL13. These findings suggest that SAg-driven dysregulation of tonsillar immunity redirects Tfh cells toward a proliferative state, leading to B cell loss and diminished antibody production, changes that likely confer a survival advantage to superantigen-producing bacteria [ ]. It has been known for about two decades that streptococcal SAgs exhibit varying susceptibility to degradation by the cysteine protease SpeB. While SMEZ is most sensitive to degradation, other SAgs, like SpeA and SpeG, are more resistant and SpeJ is completely unaffected [ ]. A more recent study demonstrated that SpeA is not only protease-resistant but works synergistically with SpeB to induce inflammation [ ]. Despite their strong association with toxic shock syndrome, GAS SAgs do not appear to be the primary drivers of invasion but seem to function predominantly as amplifiers of pathology once invasive infection has been established. SAgs are neither necessary nor sufficient for tissue invasion and are absent from many severe invasive isolates. Their contribution appears temporally and contextually constrained, requiring high bacterial burden and systemic exposure, and might be best understood as potentiating host immune dysregulation rather than initiating disease. 2.2. Cytolysins and NAD Glycohydrolase 2.2.1. Streptolysin O (SLO) SLO belongs to the family of cholesterol-dependent pore-forming toxins which are found predominantly in Gram-positive pathogens. Pore formation is due to the self-assembly of monomers bound individually to cholesterol-rich membranes, although alternative receptors also contribute. SLO binds to a broad range of glycans and the highest affinity interactions were detected for the ABO blood group antigens, with the highest affinity observed for the group B type IV pentasaccharide [ ]. Receptor binding is followed by dimerisation and oligomerisation, inducing rapid, dose-dependent apoptosis in many human cells, in particular macrophages and neutrophils, and protecting the bacteria from phagocytic killing [ ]. SLO promotes bacterial escape from the GAS-containing vacuole (GCV) into the macrophage cytosol and cytosolic growth, despite autophagy receptor recruitment [ ]. In neutrophils, SLO has the capacity to suppress oxidative burst and other key neutrophil functions, including degranulation, directed migration, and formation of NETs, together promoting neutrophil resistance [ ]. SLO functions synergistically with NAD glycohydrolase (NADase), a co-expressed enzyme that depletes the cellular energy stores of host cells. The two toxins form stable complexes in solution, enhancing SLO-mediated cytotoxicity and contributing to GAS virulence [ ]. Moreover, SLO and NADase disrupt host cell physiology by inducing Golgi fragmentation and inhibiting anterograde transport, thereby increasing bacterial translocation across epithelial barriers [ ]. Cyclic-di-AMP produced by GAS can pass through streptolysin O pores into macrophages, where it activates a stimulator of interferon genes (STING) and triggers a type I IFN response. However, this response is suppressed by invasive strains expressing enzymatically active NADase. Patient analyses from necrotising GAS soft tissue infections show that a STING variant with reduced cyclic-di-AMP binding, combined with high bacterial NADase activity, creates a “perfect storm” associated with poor outcomes. In contrast, efficient and uninhibited STING-mediated type I interferon (IFN) responses are linked to protection against harmful inflammation [ ]. The central role of SLO in GAS pathogenicity is further underscored by hypervirulent strains that produce elevated levels of the toxin, resulting in enhanced hemolysis, reduced dendritic cell (DC) viability, and increased TNF and MCP-1 production by DCs [ ]. 2.2.2. Streptolysin S (SLS) SLS is a 2.7 kDa ribosomally synthesised, post-translationally modified peptide with a broad cytolytic spectrum, which includes erythrocytes, leukocytes, platelets, and even sub-cellular organelles. SLS is responsible for the typical β-hemolytic phenotype seen around colonies of GAS, when cultured on blood agar [ ]. SLS induces osmotic lysis of red blood cells by disrupting the chloride–bicarbonate exchanger band 3, leading to rapid Cl − influx and subsequent cell rupture [ ]. More recently, SLS has also been shown to target the electroneutral sodium–bicarbonate cotransporter NBCn1 in keratinocytes, triggering NF-κB activation and cytotoxicity during GAS infection [ ]. The importance of SLS in colonisation and disease has been highlighted by studies using SLS-deficient strains, which showed a 100-fold reduction in bacterial recovery from the nasopharynx and a 10-fold reduction in bacterial burden in skin. Neutrophil depletion partially restored bacterial load in the skin but not in the nasopharynx, suggesting tissue-specific roles. In mice infected intranasally with wild-type GAS, SLS caused relocalisation and disruption of the tight junction protein ZO-1 at sites of infection, a change absent in infections with SLS-deficient strains, underscoring its role in epithelial barrier damage [ ]. Beyond epithelial disruption, SLS induces macrophage death by preventing glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β) degradation and exacerbating mitochondrial damage [ ]. SLS also contributes to immune evasion by perforating the phagolysosomal membrane to allow leakage of protons and proteins like cathepsin B [ ]. It also activates nociceptor neurons, driving pain responses during infection, particularly in necrotising fasciitis. Activated nociceptors release calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) into infected tissues, which suppresses neutrophil recruitment and impairs opsonophagocytic killing of GAS [ ]. 2.3. Streptococcal Pyrogenic Exotoxin B (SpeB) Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B (SpeB) was originally mis-classified as a superantigen due to contamination of the purified sample and has been re-classified as streptococcal cysteine protease (or streptopain). SpeB has a very broad substrate spectrum and degrades many proteins secreted by GAS, including other virulence factors, like SMEZ [ ] (see above). In addition, SpeB has been shown to degrade the extracellular matrix, cytokines, chemokines, complement components, immunoglobulins, and serum protease inhibitors (reviewed in [ , ]). SpeB cleaves the extracellular domains of desmoglein-1 and -3, molecules critical for tissue integrity and cell–cell communication. In an epicutaneous infection model, lesions caused by an speB deletion mutant were significantly smaller than those produced by the wild-type strain, indicating that SpeB-mediated desmosome degradation plays a pathogenic role in the development of GAS skin infections [ ]. Nevertheless, the in vivo significance of this antibody cleavage remains debated [ ]. More recently, SpeB has been shown to trigger keratinocyte pyroptosis by cleaving Gasdermin A (GSDMA), a pore-forming member of the gasdermin family that acts as a sensor, substrate, and effector of pyroptosis. This cleavage releases an active N-terminal fragment that initiates pyroptosis. Caspase-independent cleavage of GSDMA by SpeB is highly selective and requires SpeB to enter the cytosol of the infected cell. In mice, genetic deficiency of Gsdma1 impaired immune responses to GAS, leading to uncontrolled bacterial dissemination and death. Thus, GSDMA functions simultaneously as a sensor and substrate of SpeB, as well as an effector that induces pyroptosis, providing a streamlined, one-molecule mechanism for host recognition and control of a highly virulent pathogen [ , ]. 2.4. Streptokinase (SK) Streptokinase (SK) is a secreted protein that activates host plasminogen, converting it into plasmin. This fibrinolytic activity enables GAS to degrade fibrin clots and extracellular matrix components, facilitating bacterial spread through tissues and evasion of host immune defences. In contrast to other plasminogen activators, SK lacks intrinsic enzymatic activity. By hijacking the host’s own proteolytic system, SK enhances invasiveness and contributes to severe diseases such as necrotising fasciitis and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome. Its potent activity has also been harnessed clinically as a thrombolytic agent for dissolving blood clots in cardiovascular medicine, though its bacterial origin limits its widespread use today (reviewed in [ ]). GAS recruits plasminogen and plasmin to its surface through several cell wall-associated proteins, including M proteins, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, and streptococcal enolase. Together with streptokinase, these factors generate both soluble and surface-bound plasmin activity, enhancing the pathogen’s invasive potential. A more recent study has shown that SK acts synergistically with plasminogen-binding M protein (PAM) to enhance plasminogen activation, leading to fibrin clot dissolution and keratinocyte wound layer retraction, thereby facilitating bacterial dissemination [ ]. Until recently, the mechanism by which GAS embedded within fibrin clots accessed plasminogen for dissolution was unclear. Live imaging studies by Vu and colleagues showed that bacteria entrapped in clots can persist in a dormant state until plasminogen becomes available to trigger fibrinolysis. Using a 3D endothelial microfluidic model, they further demonstrated that GAS can effectively induce fibrinolysis in an endothelial setting, enabling its dissemination into the bloodstream [ ]. During the early stages of GAS infection, SK aids bacterial evasion of innate immunity by promoting plasmin-mediated degradation of host defence molecules, including the antimicrobial peptide LL-37, complement component C3b, and histones [ , , ]. In addition, SK can trigger contact system activation at the bacterial surface, leading to cleavage of high-molecular-weight kininogen and release of bradykinin, thereby amplifying inflammation during infection [ ]. 2.5. Each GAS strain secretes at least one extracellular DNase and most strains produce several of these enzymes. An isogenic triple mutant of a contemporary M1 strain was less virulent compared to the Wt strain in two mouse invasive disease models [ ]. The important contribution of DNases to GAS disease progression was also demonstrated in a study that used Δ spd and ΔsdaD2 deletion mutants to show that infected mice survived better than those infected with WT GAS and that degradation of the DNA backbone structure of NETs plays an important role [ ]. Furthermore, DNA degradation by Sda1 destroyed CpG-rich DNA, a ligand for toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9). This prevented IFN-α and TNF secretion from murine macrophages, indicating that Sda1 suppresses TLR9-mediated immune responses and macrophage bactericidal activity [ ].
